strengths: The problem has an identifiable audience in contextual and combinatorial bandits: changing arm availability, semi-bandit feedback, and approximate optimization arise in useful applications.

The algorithm is understandable and modular, combining GP confidence bounds with an optimization oracle. The relationship between batch posterior covariance and information gain offers useful theoretical insight.

The experiments cover three settings, report five-run variability, and investigate kernel lengthscales, inducing-point counts, and runtime. They provide evidence of performance gains over the tested partition-based baselines in several regimes.
weaknesses: Necessary: repair the adaptive-sampling argument underlying Lemma 1 (Appendix A, p. 21, Eqs. 16–17). A deterministic policy still selects random contexts through its dependence on noisy observations; the selected contexts are not determined by preceding contexts alone. Conditional entropy generally involves an expectation over the history-dependent covariance, whereas the proof identifies it with a realized log-determinant sum. A pathwise argument using the block determinant identity appears feasible, but the supplied reasoning does not adequately justify this central step in the high-probability guarantee.

Necessary: correct the explicit parameter dependence in Corollary 1 and reconcile it with Table 1. Substituting the cited Matérn information-gain rate at n = KT into Theorem 1 gives, up to logarithms and fixed constants, sqrt(λ*(K) + σ²) times (KT)^((D+ν)/(D+2ν)). The stated sqrt(K) dependence omits an additional polynomial factor unless K is treated as a suppressed constant. Also, Eq. 4 depends on the per-round feasibility constraints, so it is not simply the usual maximum information gain over the union of available contexts.

Necessary: document the reward and probability conventions used in the experiments. Under the Gaussian-noise model, Simulation I's log(1 + sum of outcomes) is undefined with positive probability. In Simulation III, GP upper confidence bounds can exceed one, although TIM+ requires valid edge probabilities; clipping or another transformation is not specified. These details affect whether the described experiments can be reproduced and interpreted. The Bernoulli-feedback and sparse-GP experiments should also be explicitly distinguished from the assumptions supporting the theorem.

Necessary: narrow the empirical conclusions. MovieLens supplies contexts and graph structure, but outcomes are generated from a hand-specified response function, and the benchmark itself uses an approximation oracle. Approaching that benchmark demonstrates strong performance in this semi-synthetic experiment, not the claimed 'optimal performance.' Broad superiority and online-scalability claims also exceed comparisons with two partition-based baselines and short horizons where sparse updates still take hundreds of seconds per round.

Optional: comparisons with the closely related GP-bandit approaches already cited, together with kernel-sensitivity experiments, would strengthen practical guidance. Acceptance does not require a new algorithm or state-of-the-art performance; my leaning-reject recommendation concerns the unresolved justification and reporting of the current claims.
